e.t: Bilhan is a Hebrew personal name, functioning as the proper name of individuals in the Old Testament. It appears four times across three verses, and English Bible renderings preserve it as “Bilhan” rather than translating it into a descriptive word. The name occurs once in Genesis and three times in 1 Chronicles. Its precise significance as a personal name is not defined in the available passages, so the supported meaning is the name itself: Bilhan.

e.t: Baal Perazim is a Hebrew name, rendered “Baal” and “Perazim.” It is not presented here as an ordinary action or quality word, but as a named designation occurring in the Old Testament. The name appears eight times, concentrated in two verses: 2 Samuel 5:20 and 1 Chronicles 14:11. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This Hebrew word means “son.” It identifies a male child or descendant in the Old Testament passages where it appears. The word occurs eight times across seven verses, all within the Hebrew Bible, with its recorded uses found in Ezra and Daniel. Its ordinary meaning remains simple and direct: it refers to a son, while the surrounding verse determines the particular person being identified. The supplied references include Ezra 5:1–2, Ezra 6:14, and several passages in Daniel.

Gideoni is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Gideoni.” It identifies a particular man rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all within Numbers, from Numbers 1:11 through Numbers 10:24. Since the available information gives the name but not a separate definition or name-meaning explanation, its clear function is to identify the person called Gideoni in those passages.

This Hebrew word refers to “cud,” the food an animal brings back up and chews again. It is used in the Old Testament’s descriptions of animals, especially in passages that distinguish animals according to whether they have this feature. The word occurs 11 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Leviticus and Deuteronomy. Its normal function is as a noun naming this part of an animal’s digestive process.

This Hebrew word is a rare term whose precise meaning cannot be stated from the available lexical information. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Job 6:2, so its ordinary use cannot be established by comparing multiple passages. The verse reference identifies where it occurs, but no verse text or explicit definition is available here. Its identity as a Hebrew source word is established, while its English meaning remains undetermined in this record.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a raised natural height of land—a “mount” or “mountains.” It is used broadly in the Old Testament for prominent elevated places, whether mentioned singly or as a range. The word occurs 547 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Malachi, showing that mountains are a recurring part of biblical geography and imagery. Its exact significance in any passage depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word is a proper name, rendered “Hagaba” or “Hagabah,” rather than a common word describing an idea, action, or quality. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, once in Ezra and once in Nehemiah. The available wording identifies the name, but does not establish a broader lexical meaning or explain the person or group associated with it. Its occurrences are recorded at Ezra 2:45 and Nehemiah 7:48.

This Hebrew verb means “renew”—to make something new again, restore it, or bring it back into fresh condition. It can describe renewing a people’s commitment, restoring a city or structure, or asking God to renew a person inwardly. The word occurs 10 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its central idea is consistent while its object may differ. As a verb, it expresses an action performed on something that needs restoration or fresh vitality.

This word means “living.” It describes a person or being as alive, and it can function as a description of life rather than as the name of a particular person or object. In its Hebrew Old Testament use, it appears seven times, six of them in Daniel and once in Ezra. Its occurrences include descriptions connected with human life and with the living God. The word’s precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains living existence.

This Hebrew word refers to a “declaration”—something spoken or formally made known. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in Job 13:17. The word’s basic sense points to a communicated statement that others are expected to hear or give attention to. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding words and passage, but its established meaning is limited to this idea of a declaration rather than a broader set of inferred meanings.

This Hebrew word refers to a “stork,” a particular bird. It appears six times in the Old Testament corpus, each time in a different verse. Its uses include the lists of birds in Leviticus and Deuteronomy, poetic references in Job and Psalms, and prophetic passages in Jeremiah and Zechariah. Thus, its ordinary scriptural function is a straightforward noun naming the stork rather than an abstract idea or action.

Its precise reference in any verse depends on the surrounding passage and the place being described.

Its precise force in any particular verse comes from the surrounding sentence, but its consistent lexical sense is “fierce.”

e.t: “Jehudi” is a personal name identifying an individual in the Hebrew Bible. It is not presented here as a general description or action word, but as the designation of a particular person. The name occurs four times in three verses, all within Jeremiah 36:14–23. Its repeated use in this short passage shows that the same named individual is being referred to across the account. The precise role of Jehudi in each verse depends on the surrounding verse text.

This Hebrew word means “barefoot,” describing a person who has no footwear. It functions as a description of bodily condition or appearance rather than an action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs five times, including passages in 2 Samuel, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. The repeated rendering “barefoot” gives the clearest ordinary meaning, while the precise significance in any particular verse depends on its surrounding passage.

It commonly functions as the predicate, telling what someone or something could do, endure, or be. The word occurs 194 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its ordinary sense appears across many kinds of statements rather than belonging to one narrow setting. Its precise force in any particular verse comes from the surrounding sentence and passage.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to someone who is "fatherless"—a person lacking a living or present father to provide protection and care. In the Old Testament, it is used for people who may be especially vulnerable and therefore receive attention in commands about justice, provision, celebration, and community responsibility. The word occurs 42 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a consistent concern for the fatherless rather than a merely occasional reference. Its normal meaning focuses on a person’s family situation and need for protection.

This Hebrew word refers to “windows,” meaning openings in a building that allow people to look or direct their attention outward. It names a physical feature rather than an action or abstract idea. In the Hebrew Old Testament data, it occurs once, in Daniel 6:10. The term therefore identifies a place or architectural feature rather than describing what someone does, feels, or believes. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and context.

This Hebrew word refers to the “Carmites,” a named group associated with the family or line identified in the Old Testament. It occurs once in the Hebrew Bible, at Numbers 26:6, and the English rendering is consistently “Carmites.” Because no verse text or broader contextual details are available here, the word’s clear lexical role is as a group designation rather than a description of an action, quality, or spiritual theme.

This Hebrew word can refer to something “flaming” or to “enchantments,” with the surrounding passage determining which sense is intended. It appears twice in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus: once in Genesis 3:24 and once in Exodus 7:11. These two uses show that the word’s meaning is connected either with fiery imagery or with enchantment practices, but the word should not be assigned one English rendering in every passage. Its precise sense depends on its sentence and context.

Migron is a Hebrew place name, referring to a location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in 1 Samuel 14:2 and Isaiah 10:28, and is rendered “Migron” in the available English renderings. Because the word functions as a proper name, its basic meaning is the identification of that place; the surrounding verse and passage are needed to understand what happens there in each occurrence.

This Hebrew word means “salvation.” It functions as a noun, naming salvation rather than describing an action or person. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 68:20, so its ordinary meaning is established from that single occurrence and its English rendering. It should therefore be understood as a name for salvation in the sentence, while the wider Psalm supplies the specific setting and emphasis.

“Stringed” describes something made or equipped with strings, functioning as a descriptive word rather than naming an action. In this Hebrew Old Testament entity, the term appears twice, both in Psalms, and its recorded uses are Psalm 45:8 and Psalm 150:4. The exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its ordinary lexical contribution points to something involving strings, especially in a musical setting.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a mitre, or turban—a head covering worn as part of the priestly clothing. In the Old Testament, it is especially associated with the high priest’s garments and appears in descriptions of how that head covering was made, placed, and dedicated. The word occurs 12 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, chiefly in Exodus and Leviticus, with one later occurrence in Ezekiel. Its use consistently points to a specific ceremonial head covering rather than to headwear in general.

Ellasar is a proper name, rendered “Ellasar,” rather than a descriptive word with a stated meaning. It identifies the same named entity each time it appears in the Hebrew Old Testament. This word occurs twice, both times in Genesis 14, at Genesis 14:1 and Genesis 14:9. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself supplies no further lexical definition or contextual detail.

The word refers to the Mishraites, functioning as a proper group name rather than a general description. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 2:53. Because it is a people-name, its meaning is primarily identifying: it marks the group being mentioned, rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract idea. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain its specific role there.

e.t: This word means “prophet,” referring to a person recognized in the Old Testament as a messenger who speaks in connection with God. It can refer to one prophet or to prophets as a group, depending on the sentence. The word appears 316 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing that prophets are a recurring part of Israel’s scriptural history. Its usage is especially associated with speech, divine messages, and the testing of whether a claimed message is true.

This Hebrew word means “branch,” referring to a young growth that comes from a tree or plant. It can describe a literal branch or shoot, and its recurring use in Isaiah and Daniel gives it a concrete botanical sense within the Old Testament. The word occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in separate verses. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains a branch growing from a larger plant.

This word functions as a designation for the “Nethinims,” a named group referred to in the Hebrew Old Testament. It appears only once in this corpus, in Ezra 7:24, so its ordinary lexical use is narrowly represented. The available rendering identifies the group by name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. Its precise significance in Ezra depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This Hebrew word means “black” and identifies a color. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Esther 1:6, so its ordinary lexical sense is clear but is illustrated in only one passage. The word functions as a description of the color associated with something in a sentence. It does not itself name an object, action, or person; it identifies the color of what is being described.

This Hebrew word means “covered.” It describes something being covered or enclosed rather than left exposed. In its six Old Testament occurrences, it is used in descriptions involving structures and surfaces, and it can also describe a person as seated beneath or within a covering. Its ordinary function is to express the condition or placement of something under a covering. The surrounding verse determines exactly what provides the covering and what is covered.

Its ordinary meaning remains specific: it identifies an uncircumcised person or people, rather than naming a separate action, object, or emotion.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to a “stone,” or to “stones” when more than one is intended. It normally names a hard piece of rock used as an object, material, marker, or building element. The word occurs 273 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing broad use across descriptions, commands, and events. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on how the surrounding sentence uses the stone or stones.

Ozem is a personal name, rendered as “Ozem,” rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in 1 Chronicles 2. Its role is to identify a person within that chapter’s family records. Because no separate lexical definition is provided, the clearest meaning is the name itself: Ozem. Its precise significance beyond identifying the person is not established by these occurrences alone.

This Hebrew word means “watchtower.” It is a noun naming a raised structure associated with watching or keeping lookout. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 21:5. The word therefore has a narrow attested range in this corpus, and its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. Its basic lexical idea remains a watchtower: a place identified by its lookout function.

Koa is a proper name, not a general term describing an action, quality, or object. It is rendered “Koa” and appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezekiel 23:23. No broader descriptive sense is given for the name, so it is best understood as identifying the entity named in that passage. Its precise referent requires the surrounding verse text and context.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “uttermost.” It identifies a part or position at the far end of something, functioning as a noun rather than naming an action or person. It is used 36 times in the Old Testament, including descriptions of constructed objects and locations within them. The word therefore helps specify where an outermost portion belongs in relation to the larger object or arrangement being described.

This Hebrew word carries the approved meanings “cause” and “corners.” Its exact sense is therefore shaped by how it functions in its sentence: it can be rendered as an action that causes something, or in connection with corners. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in Leviticus 14:41 and once in Ezekiel 46:22. These two occurrences show that the word’s ordinary rendering can differ according to context, while retaining the ideas represented by “cause” and “corners.”

This word functions as a proper name, rendered “Karka.” It identifies a particular place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 15:3. Because no verse text or broader context is available here, its precise location or significance cannot be explained further; the supported meaning is the name itself, Karka.

This Hebrew noun means “company,” referring to people considered together as a collective gathering. It functions as a naming word rather than an action or description. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Psalms: Psalm 55:14 and Psalm 64:2. The exact force of the word in either verse depends on the surrounding Hebrew sentence and passage, but its basic reference is a company of people.

This Hebrew word is an uncommon term whose precise meaning cannot be stated responsibly from the available lexical information. It occurs only once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at 2 Chronicles 22:5, and no direct lexical definition or meaning term is available. Its role in that verse must therefore be settled from the verse text and surrounding passage, rather than from this word record alone.

This Hebrew word means “meet,” functioning as a descriptive term in a sentence. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, with its only recorded occurrence in Ezra 4:14. Because the available wording gives only this single rendering and no verse text, the word’s precise force in that sentence depends on its surrounding context. Its basic sense remains the idea expressed by “meet,” without adding further translation alternatives.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to an “earthquake,” a violent movement affecting the ground. It is used 17 times in the Old Testament, including descriptions connected with the Lord’s acts and prophetic events. Its usage can also portray powerful disturbance or trembling in created things, while keeping the central idea of an earthquake. The word appears in speech and command contexts, showing that such an event may be announced, described, or presented as something that occurs. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “praise.” It functions as an action word, describing the expression of honor or acclaim. In its Old Testament use, it commonly presents praise as something directed toward God, including calls for people to praise him. The word occurs 11 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with most occurrences found in Psalms. Its exact force in a particular sentence depends on the surrounding words, but its central idea remains the act of praising.

Shebah is a Hebrew proper name, rendered as “Shebah,” rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Genesis 26:33. Because it is a name, its significance depends on the person or place it identifies in that passage, while the word itself primarily serves as a designation. Its normal lexical function is therefore naming, not expressing a broader idea or instruction.

This Hebrew word means “bruise,” expressing an action that affects another person or thing. It functions as an action word rather than a name or description. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs four times across three verses, appearing in Genesis, Job, and Psalms. Its use in Genesis 3:15 is connected with other words in the verse through several relationships, showing that it participates directly in the verse’s stated action. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its specific force in each occurrence.

This Hebrew verb means “rejoice”: to express or experience gladness and joyful delight. It describes a response of happiness in various situations, including people rejoicing and even an animal showing eagerness. The word occurs 27 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it represents a familiar biblical expression of joy rather than a rare or technical idea. In several passages, God is presented as rejoicing over his people and their prosperity, showing that the word can describe deep, active delight, not merely quiet satisfaction.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “gray” or “old” age, especially the visible signs of growing older. It can describe gray hair or the advanced age of a person. In the Old Testament, it occurs 19 times, including passages about a person reaching the end of life, a father’s grief over possible loss, and the honor due to the aged. Its central idea is age expressed through grayness, maturity, or the later years of life.

This Hebrew word is a name rendered “Shechem.” It identifies a person or place rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament data, it occurs three times: in Numbers 26:31, Joshua 17:2, and 1 Chronicles 7:19. Since it functions as a name, the surrounding verse determines which bearer or location named Shechem is intended in a particular passage.

This Hebrew word refers to a “palm.” It is used as a noun for palm trees or palm-shaped designs, especially in descriptions of the temple and its decorations. The word occurs 20 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with many uses in Ezekiel’s descriptions and several in the accounts of Solomon’s temple. Its surrounding wording can show whether the reference is to a living tree or an artistic representation, but the central meaning remains the palm form itself.

This Hebrew verb means “tread,” describing the action of stepping on or pressing down upon something. It can express physical trampling, but its wider use may describe bringing something under forceful control or crushing opposition. The word occurs 12 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including several Psalms and passages in Isaiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being acted upon and the surrounding sentence.
